analysis.one_liner: Bans importing, making, selling, buying, or transferring handguns, except for police, military, and licensed pistol clubs.
analysis.headline: The bill to outlaw civilian handgun sales was introduced by one House member with a single cosponsor, sent to a crime subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime to import, manufacture, sell, buy, transfer, receive, or transport any handgun. Exceptions would cover the armed forces, police and government agencies, and handgun activities that the Treasury Secretary authorized for licensed importers, dealers, and pistol clubs. Current owners could voluntarily hand their guns to law enforcement and get paid the gun's fair market value, or at least $25, and the ban would take effect one year after passage.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to handgun violence, if the bill's premise holds that cutting off the civilian supply of handguns reduces shootings. The bill's own findings argue handguns play a role in homicide, aggravated assault, and armed robbery far out of proportion to their share of guns, and that restricting them to law enforcement and military uses would significantly reduce violent crime.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of handgun violence

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any person to import, manufacture, sell, buy, transfer, receive, or transport any handgun.

Exempts the armed forces, law enforcement, and federal or state agencies, and lets the Treasury Secretary allow limited licensed activity by dealers and pistol clubs, for curio, museum, or collection purposes.
Lets owners voluntarily deliver handguns to law enforcement and receive payment equal to the gun's fair market value, or $25, whichever is more, upon proof of lawful ownership.

The bill's findings state that roughly 66 million handguns are in private hands, that they are used in homicides, assaults, and robberies out of proportion to their numbers, and that restricting them to noncivilian purposes would significantly reduce violent crime.

analysis.who_pays: Current handgun owners, who could no longer legally sell or transfer their guns and could keep them only outside the law; the firearms industry, which would lose the civilian handgun market; and target shooters, who would have to shoot through a licensed club that keeps the guns under the club's control when not in use.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun owners and the gun industry

drawbacks.text: The ban effectively ends civilian handgun ownership: buying, selling, and even giving a handgun away would be a federal crime, and licensed pistol clubs must keep members' handguns locked under the club's control whenever they are not in use at the club.

The bill's findings dismiss the value of handguns for home defense, asserting that defensive purposes 'can be adequately accomplished by other means' — a judgment the millions of handgun owners who keep guns for protection rejected.

Compensation is only for owners who volunteer to turn in their guns; everyone else would hold an asset they could not legally sell or transfer, and the buyback fund is paid first out of club licensing fees with the rest from general revenues.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it worked as its findings predicted, the bill would have addressed handgun violence at its supply source rather than one sale at a time. But it is one of the most sweeping gun restrictions ever introduced: it would disarm ordinary owners of a constitutionally contested category of weapon, concentrate all civilian handgun use in Treasury-licensed clubs, and depend heavily on one cabinet officer's discretion over exceptions. The cost to tens of millions of existing owners and a lawful industry is real, and the record here contains no evidence about how well such a ban would actually reduce crime.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sidney Yates introduced the Handgun Control Act of 1993 in the House on March 25, 1993.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced.
On April 5, 1993, it was sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice, where its action history ends.
No further action was taken before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, so the full House never voted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Handgun owners keep full legal ability to buy, sell, and transfer their guns, and firearms manufacturers and dealers keep the civilian handgun market. No buyback or licensing regime was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Handgun owners and the gun industry

for.name: Sidney Yates
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban civilian handgun commerce and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill at full-committee level and referred it to its crime subcommittee; never scheduled a markup or vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 5, 1993; the bill's action history ends there.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to ban civilian handgun ownership during this era.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats put their names on the bill — the sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor [S4] — and no vote was ever taken that would show where the House or either party actually stood.

industries.note: The bill outlaws every civilian handgun sale and transfer, ending the commercial handgun market; only Secretary-approved activity for clubs, agencies, and collections would continue. Its loss of revenue corresponds to the public safety gain the bill pursues.

The bill makes Treasury-licensed pistol clubs the only legal channel for civilian recreational handgun use, with a $25 annual fee, recordkeeping, and inspection requirements, and with club handguns kept locked under the club's control between uses.
